BONA FIDE WAGE DISPUTE — UNDISPUTED PORTION MUST STILL BE PAID
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
Re: Dispute Over Final Wages — Jordan Lee

This document concerns wages that Acme, Inc. owes to Jordan Lee as of September 30, 2026, where some or all of the amount claimed is disputed.

California Labor Code section 206 addresses what happens when an employer disputes the amount of wages it owes a discharged or resigning employee: it does not resolve the dispute itself, but it sets a rule for what the employer must do about the portion it does not dispute while the dispute over the rest continues. This is distinct from Labor Code section 206.5's separate rule prohibiting an employer from requiring an employee to release a wage claim as a condition of being paid wages the employer already concedes are due — a rule this project's separate Prohibition on Requiring a Release as a Condition of Wage Payment information sheet addresses in full and which this document does not repeat. This document is also distinct from this project's Final Paycheck Delivery Method and Location information sheet, which addresses how and where final wages must be delivered rather than what happens when the amount owed is disputed, and from this project's Final Wage Payment / Waiting-Time Penalty Demand Letter, which addresses the deadline for paying undisputed final wages and the penalty for missing it, not the separate question of a disputed amount addressed here.

AMOUNTS CLAIMED, CONCEDED, AND DISPUTED
For this separation, the wages at issue are described as follows:

Total amount Jordan Lee claims is owed: $3,200.00

Amount Acme, Inc. concedes is due: $2,100.00

Amount Acme, Inc. disputes: $1,100.00

THE EMPLOYER MUST PAY THE UNDISPUTED PORTION OF WAGES DESPITE A DISPUTE OVER THE REST
When an employer and a discharged or resigning employee disagree about the amount of wages owed, California law requires the employer to pay — without condition, and within the deadline that otherwise applies to final wages — whatever amount of wages, or part of the wages, the employer itself concedes is due. This rule means an employer does not get to withhold an entire final paycheck merely because part of the amount claimed is disputed: the conceded portion must be paid regardless of the ongoing dispute over the balance, and paying it does not resolve, waive, or limit the employee's remedies as to the disputed remainder, which the employee remains free to pursue.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "In case of a dispute over wages, the employer shall pay, without condition and within the time set by this article, all wages, or parts thereof, conceded by him to be due, leaving to the employee all remedies he might otherwise be entitled to as to any balance claimed."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 206(a), Lab. Code § 206, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=206.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the pay-the-undisputed-portion rule — not a claim about which state's law governs this particular dispute, and not a claim that any particular amount here is actually conceded, disputed, or owed. This is a single statutory subdivision (§ 206(a)); a separate clause in this document quotes subdivision (b) of the same section, so that citation is not independent of this one. The statute does not define what makes a dispute a genuine, good-faith one as opposed to a pretextual withholding, and this clause does not attempt to draw that line; a California Court of Appeal decision addressing a related distinction between wages conceded to be due and a bona fide dispute over wages — discussed in this project's separate Prohibition on Requiring a Release as a Condition of Wage Payment information sheet in the context of Labor Code section 206.5 — is not restated here, since that document already covers it and this clause does not duplicate it. This clause also does not work through how the deadline cross-referenced here ("within the time set by this article") interacts with the specific discharge-and-quit deadlines of Labor Code sections 201 and 202, which this project's separate documents address.

ONE REMEDY FOR THE DISPUTED BALANCE: A LABOR COMMISSIONER DETERMINATION
Section 206 also describes one specific remedy available for the disputed balance the employee remains free to pursue: if, after an investigation and hearing, the Labor Commissioner determines the validity of the employee's wage claim, the amount determined to be due becomes due and payable within 10 days after the employer receives notice of that determination. An employer that has the ability to pay and willfully fails to pay within that 10-day window is liable, in addition to any other applicable penalty, for treble the amount of any damages the employee suffers as a direct and foreseeable consequence of that failure to pay.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "If, after an investigation and hearing, the Labor Commissioner has determined the validity of any employee’s claim for wages, the claim is due and payable within 10 days after receipt of notice by the employer that such wages are due. Any employer having the ability to pay who willfully fails to pay such wages within 10 days shall, in addition to any other applicable penalty, pay treble the amount of any damages accruing to the employee as a direct and foreseeable consequence of such failure to pay."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 206(b), Lab. Code § 206, subd. (b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=206.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of this specific remedy pathway — not a claim about which state's law governs this particular claim, and not a claim that any particular claim here has been, or will be, investigated or determined by the Labor Commissioner. This is a single statutory subdivision (§ 206(b)); the prior clause in this document quotes subdivision (a) of the same section, so that citation is not independent of this one. This clause describes only this administrative-determination-and-treble-damages remedy; it is one of "all remedies" an employee is left free to pursue under subdivision (a), not the only one — an employee may instead, or also, have other remedies (such as a civil action) that this clause does not describe. This clause does not describe the Labor Commissioner's investigation-and-hearing procedure itself, does not determine whether any particular employer has the ability to pay or has acted willfully within the meaning of this subdivision, and does not address how "damages" here relates to the waiting-time penalty under a separate statute, which this project's separate Final Wage Payment / Waiting-Time Penalty Demand Letter document addresses.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Please sign below to acknowledge review of the information above.

Employee: Jordan Lee
Date: _______________

Employer representative (on behalf of Acme, Inc.): _______________
Date: _______________
